Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 3:5: To summarize: fulfilling the 613 commandments while the evil inclination is present in the person and he overcomes it — this is called a tzaddik. And when he fulfills them through the nullification of the evil inclination, which shows that the good character traits have been acquired as a complete second nature — this is called a complete chasid.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 3:6: There is yet another level of piety above this one, than which there is none higher, and this man is called kadosh (holy); it is mentioned in the Sefer HaTikkunim and in the Zohar in many places, and in particular in Parashat Ki Tetzei, in the Ra'aya Meheimna (281a), and this is its language: 'And it was not for nothing that the Holy One, blessed be He, said: Whoever occupies himself with Torah and with acts of loving-kindness and prays with the congregation, I credit it to him as though he had redeemed Me and My children from among the nations of the world — and how many people occupy themselves with Torah, and yet the Holy One, blessed be He, has not been redeemed... but [the reason is] as they have established, that a chasid is only one who does chesed with his Maker — for when Israel sinned, the Holy One, blessed be He, drove out the King's Son and the Matron together with them into exile, and whoever returns in repentance and does an act of loving-kindness with the Shechinah, through Torah and all its commandments, his intention being solely to redeem the Shechinah — this one does chesed with his Maker...'
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 3:7: <small>[Gloss — And it was not for nothing that the Holy One, blessed be He, said: Whoever occupies himself with Torah and with acts of loving-kindness and prays with the congregation, I credit it to him as though he had redeemed Me and My children from among the nations of the world. And though people occupy themselves with Torah, the Holy One, blessed be He, has still not been redeemed — the reason for this is that a chasid is only one who does chesed with his Maker, for at the time Israel sinned, the Holy One, blessed be He, exiled His children and the Shechinah together with them. And whoever returns in repentance and does an act of loving-kindness with the Shechinah, occupying himself with the Torah and its commandments, with the sole intention of redeeming the Shechinah, does chesed with his Maker]</small>:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 3:8: Now this is what Scripture means (Deuteronomy 32:18), "You neglected the Rock who bore you," and it is written (Psalms 68:35), "Ascribe strength to God," and this is what they said (Berachot 17a), Rabbi Yehuda says: 'Happy is one whose labor is in Torah and who gives satisfaction to his Maker' — for his labor in the Torah is not in order to receive any reward for himself, but rather to give satisfaction to his Maker. And it is written of Him (Isaiah 63:9), "In all their affliction, He was afflicted." And in every place to which Israel was exiled, the Shechinah went with them — she is our mother, of whom it is said (ibid. 50:1), "and for your transgressions your mother was sent away" — she is called our Maker (yotzreinu), as it is written, "the Rock who bore (yeladcha) you." This is why it says "satisfaction to his Maker" and not "to the Holy One, blessed be He."
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 3:9: It follows that when he occupies himself with Torah and mitzvot and good character traits — called a chasid, as mentioned above — if the intention of receiving some reward has become mixed into it, he is a chasid for himself; as it is written (Proverbs 11:17), "A man of kindness benefits his own soul" — for in fulfilling the commandments, he does kindness to his own soul. Therefore he is not called a chasid but rather an ish chesed (a man of kindness), for the kindness is toward the man himself, who benefits his own soul; but one who does kindness with his Maker is called a chasid and kadosh, since he has been refined of every kind of impurity and has sanctified himself with His holiness, blessed be He. For the term kedushah (holiness) is a term of preparation and readiness, as in (Numbers 11:18), "Sanctify yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat" — for he makes himself a chariot for His holiness, blessed be He, and is not concerned for his own honor but only for the honor of his Maker, as mentioned above.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 3:10: And this is what Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair intended in what he said (Mishnah, end of Sotah): "Abstinence (perishut) brings one to purity... and holiness (kedushah) brings one to piety (chasidut), and piety brings one to the Holy Spirit" — for this is a complete piety that comes after holiness, and it is this that brings one to the Holy Spirit, for he becomes wholly attached, and merits the revelation of the secrets of the Torah and to prophesy future things, as Rabbi Meir said (Avot 6:5), "Whoever occupies himself with Torah lishmah (for its own sake)" — meaning, for the sake of the Torah, which is [a Name of] the Holy One, blessed be He Himself, for the whole Torah consists of the Names of the Holy One, blessed be He — "merits many things... and the secrets of the Torah are revealed to him, and he becomes like an ever-strengthening spring..."
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:1-3: An explanation of the level of the tzaddik in detail:

This is that he should hasten with all his strength to complete, as much as possible, the fulfillment of the 613 commandments in this time. And since there are many opinions regarding the counting of the commandments, I will first arrange them according to the view of Maimonides, of blessed memory, and after them I will arrange what the other commentators and the Sefer HaZohar add, both regarding the count of the Torah's positive commandments and the positive commandments of Rabbinic origin, and I will divide them into five categories:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:4: The first, commandments applicable at the time of prayer on every weekday. The second, commandments dependent on time. The third, commandments that require the opportunity to present itself to a person. The fourth, commandments that a person must actively seek out in order to fulfill them. The fifth, commandments that are not within a person's power to seek out, unless the Holy One, blessed be He, brings them to his hand.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:5: The first: To know that there is a God, in the verse "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God"; to declare His unity by saying "the Lord is One"; to make tzitzit and wrap oneself in them; to bind tefillin, according to the view of Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam, [and] shel rosh (the head-tefillin) primarily; to bind the tefillin of the arm in the manner mentioned; to recite the Shema twice each day; to pray the Amidah of eighteen benedictions every day; to remember every day what Amalek did to us, when one says "Amen, yehei shemei rabba," as it is written (Exodus 17:16), "for a hand is on the throne of the Lord (kes Yah)," and when one says "and bring us near, our King, to Your great Name"; to confess every day after the Amidah and in the blessing "Shema koleinu"; and to bless the people of Israel through the Priestly Blessing every day.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:6: The second: To sanctify [the day] over wine at the entrance of the Sabbath and to make Havdalah at its departure; to rest on the Sabbath from one's labor; to nullify chametz by [renouncing it in] one's heart on the night of the fourteenth of Nisan; to recount the Exodus from Egypt in the Haggadah on the first night of Pesach; to rest from labor on the first day of Pesach; to eat matzah on the first night of Pesach; to rest on the seventh day of Pesach; to rejoice on the three pilgrimage festivals — Pesach, Shavuot, and Sukkot — and to give joy to one's wife, children, and the poor, each according to what is fitting; to count the Omer, forty-nine complete days from the beginning of the night of the sixteenth of Nisan; to rest on Shavuot; to rest on Rosh Hashanah; to hear the sound of the shofar on Rosh Hashanah; to rest on Yom Kippur; to afflict oneself [by fasting] on Yom Kippur; to rest on the first day of Sukkot; to rest on Shemini Atzeret; to dwell in a sukkah for the seven days of the festival; to take the lulav and its species, fit for use, on the first day of Sukkot.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:7: The third: To write a Torah scroll; to affix a mezuzah; to bless the Grace after Meals; to study Torah and to teach it every day; to be fruitful and multiply; to enter into marriage through kiddushin; to circumcise one's son; to separate challah from the dough in the Land of Israel; to give charity; to lend to the poor; to return a pledge at its proper time; to make a parapet [on one's roof]; to honor the kohanim; to honor Torah scholars; to honor one's father and mother; to fear one's father and mother; to love one's fellow; to love converts; to pay a hired laborer's wage at its proper time; to allow the hired laborer to eat [from the produce he handles]; to check the signs [of kashrut] of an animal; to check the signs of a fowl; to check the signs of fish and locusts; to mourn for one's relatives; "You shall surely rebuke" [your fellow]; "That which has gone out of your lips you shall keep"; to cleave to Him; "and you shall walk in His ways"; to fear the Lord; to distance oneself from sin; to love the Lord — in all the particulars our Sages, of blessed memory, mentioned.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:8: The fourth: To separate terumah gedolah; to separate terumat ma'aser; to separate the first tithe; to separate the second tithe; to give pe'ah, leket, shikhecha, peret, and olelot [to the poor]; to give the firstborn of a kosher animal to the kohen; to redeem the firstborn donkey; to break the neck of the firstborn donkey [if not redeemed]; the fourth-year fruit; the shoulder, cheeks, and stomach [given to the kohen]; the first shearing [given to the kohen]; to return a lost object; to return something stolen; to lend to a gentile with interest; to press a gentile [for repayment]; to destroy idolatry; to have honest scales, weights, and measures; "You shall surely release" [an animal in distress]; "You shall surely lift up" [a burden with your fellow]; to swear by His Name in court; to send away the mother bird; to slaughter cattle, wild animals, and fowl [properly]; to cover the blood of a wild animal or fowl; to cry out and plead in prayer, and to sound trumpets or a shofar over the community's troubles, God forbid; to rest from working the land in the Sabbatical year; to release the produce of the land in the Sabbatical year — and there is a dispute whether this is by Torah law or by Rabbinic law; to divorce by means of a get; for a Nazirite to let his hair grow; to save the pursued; for a rapist to marry the woman he raped; for one who defames his wife's honor to remain married to her all his days; to sanctify His Name, blessed be He, through self-sacrifice; to appoint judges and officers; to treat litigants equally; to testify in court; to judge conspiring witnesses; to examine witnesses; "A groom shall be free for his home for one year"; to adjudicate all the laws of annulling vows; to pay for damage one has caused another's property or for injuring another, to adjudicate damages caused by an animal that gores, and damages of tooth, pit, and fire, and damages of an unpaid bailee, a paid bailee, and a borrower, and every kind of buying and selling, and every kind of plaintiff and defendant, and the laws of inheritance; to judge a thief by requiring payment; to follow the majority.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:9: The fifth: To redeem a firstborn son; for a widow to be taken in levirate marriage by her brother-in-law; for chalitzah to be performed by the widow of one's brother [if he refuses].
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:10: And these are of Rabbinic origin:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:11: The Sabbath candle, the Chanukah candle, the reading of the Megillah, the washing of hands, eruvei chatzerot, eruvei techumin when it is for the sake of a mitzvah, eruvei tavshilin, and shittufei mevo'ot; to fast on the four fasts — Tammuz, Av, Tishrei, Tevet (and the Fast of Esther); to fast over the community's troubles.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:12: And these are the positive commandments of Torah origin according to the other commentators and the Sefer HaZohar.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:13: To remember the Exodus from Egypt in the passage of tzitzit, by day and by night; to remember the Sabbath day every day; to remember the day you stood before the Lord your God at Chorev; to remember how you provoked the Lord your God to anger in the wilderness; to remember the deed of Miriam; to bless the Torah before [studying] it; to gaze upon the tzitzit at the verse "and you shall see it"; to return in complete repentance; to fear the Lord through the morning sacrifices and songs of praise; to love the Name through "Ahavat Olam" and the verse "and you shall love the Lord your God..."; to bless Him with "Yishtabach" and "Yotzer Or" and "Yotzer HaMe'orot" and all seven blessings of the Shema recitation, morning and evening; to sanctify His Name, blessed be He, through self-sacrifice unto death, through the verse "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One"; to sanctify His Name in "Nekadesh"; to give over one's soul to death, and also to cleave to Him in falling upon one's face at the verse "To You, O Lord, I lift up my soul"; to know that the Lord is God, in the verse "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One"; to delight in the Sabbath; to make Havdalah at the departure of a festival; to recite Hallel at the known times; to swear by His Name in fulfillment of a commandment; to bless the blessing over pleasure for every kind of enjoyment; to afflict oneself on Yom Kippur through the five afflictions; to burn the chametz on the fourteenth of Nisan; "and you shall honor the presence of an elder" — a Torah scholar, young or old, and even an unlearned elder; to be modest in the bathroom; to justify Heaven's judgment over every event; to separate terumah from the best of the produce; to build a synagogue in which to pray; to destroy the name of idolatry; to mention it with contempt; to cut down an Asherah; to burn an Asherah; to break their monuments; to destroy their high places; to demolish their altars; to destroy the utensils of idolatrous worship; to separate from a woman near her menstrual period; to separate from a woman in sexual relations the moment she sees blood; to fear a Torah scholar; to circumcise the foreskin of the heart; to love rebuke; to act beyond the letter of the law; "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God"; and not to hearken to the words of astrologers; love of fellow Jews, and within it, to judge him favorably even when he is not present, and to bring peace between one person and another, and "your brother shall live with you"; to return excessive interest [that was taken]; and all the laws of saving life and every kind of remedy by which a person may live; to annul the vows of one's wife and daughter; to render legal decisions; for a judge to fulfill "keep far from a false matter"; to adjudicate the laws of partners and the division of land, and every kind of claimant and defendant.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:14: And these are positive commandments from the words of the Sages:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 4:15: To scald [non-kosher] vessels [to render them kosher]; to immerse new vessels [in a mikveh]; to search for chametz on the night of the fourteenth of Nisan; to eat maror on the first night of Pesach; to bless over every commandment, and over every miracle, and over every event that befalls him; to read from the Torah scroll at the times Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, established, on the Sabbath and on Festivals, and so on.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 5:1-3: An explanation of the level of the chasid, in a brief manner, so that these things may always stand before a person:

This explains the matters that are constantly present and that require great care, and which are also matters more grave than all the rest, as I have distilled them from the pearls of the pleasant words of our Sages, of blessed memory, in the Talmud and the Midrashim, and in Massekhet Yirat Chet and Pirkei Derech Eretz, and in the Sefer HaZohar. It has already been explained in the preceding gates that there are three levels,
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 5:4: The first, the acquisition of good character traits in the foundational soul as a complete second nature. The second, turning away from evil — the 365 negative commandments — in the intellective soul. The third, the fulfillment of the 248 positive commandments, called "doing good." And there is yet another, intermediate level, which is the acquisition of the character traits, which are also close to the negative commandments by way of asmachta and the words of tradition, that is, from the Prophets and the Writings:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 5:5: 1. The matter of the most unseemly and most grave character traits, which prevent a person's attachment to the blessed Name: pride, anger, touchiness, sadness, hatred, envy, desire for pleasures, covetousness, the seeking of authority and honor, and displaying one's good deeds to other people. Their opposites are: extreme lowliness — to the very last degree — such that he does not become angry at all, even at his own household, and does not take offense at all, and is insulted by all yet insults no one, and is joyful even in his times of trouble, and loves all creatures, even gentiles, and does not envy anything, for our days on earth are like a passing shadow; and he should hate and regard as vanity all the affairs of this world, and eat bread with salt, and so on; and he should not covet any of the vanities of this world; and he should flee with all his strength from the pursuit of authority, which buries its holders; and he should not reveal his own righteous deeds, lest he lose his reward in the World to Come and even be punished for it in Gehinnom:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 5:6: 2. The forbidden character traits. These are: evil speech, gossip-mongering, humiliating someone publicly, giving one's fellow a bad name, mockery, falsehood, flattery, deceit, idle talk, speaking of one's fellow's disgrace, glorifying oneself through another's shame, spreading strife between brothers, deriving benefit from the honor of Torah, and gazing at forbidden sights:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 5:7: 3. Regarding the negative commandments — those grave ones that carry karet, death by the hand of Heaven, and death by the court, with the desecration of the Name being the most severe of all. And it is written (Numbers 32:22), "and you shall be clear before the Lord and before Israel," and in particular regarding the sin of niddah, even in every kind of physical closeness at all; and the observance of the Sabbath in all its particulars, more than all the other commandments; to remove all flesh of forbidden fat and blood entirely; to avoid every kind of seminal impurity, even involuntary; not to use the holy Names at all, for "whoever makes use of the crown [of Torah] shall pass away"; and one who disgraces a Torah scholar, for he is called a heretic; and every kind of informing or betrayal to gentiles; and after these, the grave prohibitions such as swearing by the blessed Name, even truthfully, or a false oath, and every kind of oath; and every kind of forbidden food:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 5:8: 4. Regarding the fulfillment of positive commandments: tzitzit, tefillin, and reciting the Shema twice every day; honoring the Sabbath in all its particulars; circumcising one's son; acts of loving-kindness, visiting the sick, and welcoming guests, and bringing peace; the Amidah with the utmost intention and with joy; "causing merit to the guilty" (guiding sinners back to merit); conducting business honestly; charity; giving in secret; setting fixed times for Torah study, by day and by night, corresponding to all of them:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 5:9: 5. Regarding the observance of customs of the Torah: reciting the Shema recited over one's bed with intention; rising after midnight to mourn over the Shechinah and the destruction, and to occupy oneself with Torah; the fear of the Name always before him, so that he not sin; "in all your ways know Him"; his soul's attachment to the blessed Name should never cease, even for a moment:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:1-3: This is to include, in brief, all that has been mentioned in the preceding gates, and here will be explained the order of the conduct of the pious person, briefly, in all his deeds throughout his life, so that he not stumble. And this is its content:

"And now, my son, listen to my voice, to all that I command you: prepare to meet your God, O Israel." Each night, when you go to sleep, remember that this is the "small death" that reminds you of the great, true death, and reflect upon all the deeds you did that day, and if there were bad ones among them, confess them, for such is the way of those about to die — they confess,
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:4: and you should accept upon yourself the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven in the Shema recited over the bed, to raise your soul in unity, and afterward deposit your spirit in His hand with the verse (Psalms 31:6), "Into Your hand I entrust my spirit" — as is said of the true death (Ecclesiastes 12:7), "and the spirit shall return to God who gave it" — but now this small death, give it to Him as a deposit, to be returned to you "new every morning," to the lifeless bodies; and lie down in awe and fear, for behold, your spirit is ascending to render an account to your Maker for all your deeds, words, and thoughts of that day, and therefore let not your heart turn to idle speech or idle musings, until you fall asleep in the fear mentioned.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:5: And when you awaken from your sleep after midnight, arise quickly and briskly, light as an eagle, and wash your hands as required and proper, to remove the impure spirit from your flesh, and give Him blessing, praise, and thanksgiving for His faithfulness, blessed be He, that He did not withhold your spirit on account of your many sins, and that this was not a true, everlasting death; rather, He has restored souls to lifeless bodies, and this time even more renewed and stronger than before.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:6: And so as not to be ungrateful to Him, grieve over the exile of His mighty Shechinah and the destruction of His Temple, at the very hour when He Himself grieves, during the night watches — for your sins and the sins of your fathers caused this decline, and it has not yet been raised up from its fall; yet despite all this, He did not withhold His attention from your bad deeds, which caused her fall; and you fell upon your bed and He raised you up again, more than before, and not only that, but you will also merit the consolation of Zion, that you will rejoice with her together with all who mourn for her. Afterward, occupy yourself with the Oral Torah until the break of dawn, if you are able, for through this you draw down abundance to her and strengthen her while she is in her fallen state.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:7: And at the break of dawn, run to meet her, to the house of her prayer, for she has already preceded you there, to hear the song and the prayer that you pray to raise her from her fall and to restore her to Zion as before; and even though you cannot accomplish this alone, in stumbling you will provide a little help that day to raise her up and support her, according to your strength, and as a reward for this, she too will hear your prayer and bring your requests to a good end. Therefore, my son, let your thoughts be fixed with the utmost intent and with joy at the time you pray to raise her up and to do kindness with your Maker — and not for the sake of your own requests, for these are only meant to show before Him that, like a servant, you have no life except from your Master,
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:8: and if you call Him in truth, He too will draw near to you, as it is written (Psalms 145:18), "The Lord is near to all who call upon Him," and it is written (I Chronicles 28:9), "For the Lord searches all hearts, and understands every device and thought; if you seek Him, He will be found by you."
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:9: And especially at the time you confess before Him after the Amidah or in the blessing "Shome'a Tefillah," let it be with all your heart that you will not return to them again, for He knows both the hidden and the revealed, He sees the innermost heart and mind. And likewise in falling upon your face at the verse "To You, O Lord, I lift up my soul," resolve with all your heart to give over your soul to death for the Torah and its commandments, and thereby all your sins will be forgiven, if in truth your mouth and your heart are equal.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:10: And after you have prayed, go "from strength to strength," and set a fixed time for your Torah study lishmah, and do not exchange it or substitute anything for it, even under compulsion; and as a reward for this, "He shall appear before God in Zion" — the gates that are distinguished in the heavenly academy. Afterward, eat your meal — bread with salt and water in small measure — for "the righteous one eats to satisfy his soul" for the sustenance of the soul, and this too for the sake of Heaven, to be strong for His service, blessed be He, as it is written (Proverbs 3:6), "In all your ways know Him," and stand in awe at your table, which is likened to the altar, for you are eating at the King's table,
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:11: and in order for your table to be an atoning altar to atone for your sins, by minimizing your food to weaken the kelipah that dwells in the food your soul is nourished by, occupy yourself with some Mishnah or Psalm, and this table shall be proclaimed as "the table that is before the Lord," and the power of the evil inclination shall be weakened away from you, and the intellective soul within you shall be strengthened through the Torah, which is nourishment for that soul as well.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:12: And after your body and your soul have been nourished through eating the food that sustains and provides for us, and through the Torah, do not be ungrateful and rob the Lord, but recite the Grace after Meals for Him with great joy, like one who receives a gift from another's hand. This is what is meant in the blessing "We thank You... and for Your Torah which You have taught us, and for the food You sustain and provide for us." And as a reward for this, He will open His good storehouse to you and you will always be sustained from His generous hand:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:13: Afterward, search your heart to see whether you can fulfill some new commandment, to complete the 248 limbs of your soul, or an old commandment, to add to your reward. Afterward, go to your work or your business dealings, with complete integrity, not through deceit or fraud, and do not labor to become wealthy, only for necessary sustenance, and "make your Torah fixed and your work occasional," for one who increases his effort gains nothing extra, and one who decreases it loses nothing.
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:14: And do not accept gifts, for "he who hates gifts shall live," and the Lord makes poor and makes rich, and it is He who gives you the power to gain wealth; therefore cast your burden upon the Lord with all your heart, and He shall sustain you. And throughout the day let His fear be before you, so that you not sin in any transgression of the negative commandments, and in particular of the bad character traits, which are the leaven that sours the whole batch of dough, and especially those most commonly found in a person and which he tramples underfoot without noticing:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:15: And these are the things one must be careful of to the very last degree:
Sha'arei Kedusha, Part 1 6:16: Be careful of every kind of anger, touchiness, and pride, even toward your own household. And if someone insults you, do not answer him back; be one who is insulted but does not insult, for of this it is written (Judges 5:31), "and they who love Him are like the sun going forth in its might." Be forgiving toward whoever has wronged you, and do not feel distress even in your own heart, for it is good for you; for whoever forgives is forgiven all his own transgressions, and certainly his iniquities and sins. And if you have the eyes of understanding, you should even seek out someone to cause you distress, for it is life that you are seeking for yourself,
